chapter: Fats Waller, marriage and Indian school tours
title: Reactions of students, a college tour and his speech to Indian students
summary: Moore says how kids responded, the South Dakota college tour with Ida, and his stay-in-school speech.

blocks.x: Did the Indian children at the schools have questions about the music you were playing, did they have any aspiring musicians?

When we played Sakadone Indian School, I do a fast number everything would be awake; but when I play a slow number like I do one chorus--"Jadda"--- and these kids down in the front begin to yawn, you know, even a couple of the kids would be asleep, you know, and it's comical in there, touching, that I'd put them to sleep with my slow music. Those kids were beautiful.
I see. Did any of the teachers ever speak to you or any of the older -- the parents of the children ever --
Oh, yes, they always, I had good reception from everyone there, teachers and the super-intendents.
Did you do the Indian school tour or

Yeah, I went to the tour, only to the universities and the colleges, not Indian colleges, also University of South Dakota, the State of South Dakota only, that's when Ida was with me. This was another tour and Ida was with me and I had practically the same group and --
Was that shortly after that first tour or was that something that happened in the 1960s?
This all happened in the space of six months apart.

And Ida loved it and we got movies -- I have it downstairs and the way I rigged up this tour, I wanted to talk to the kids, Indian kids, so I'd play a set and then we had an intermission and at intermission time I'd take the mike into the center of the stage and get me a chair and I'd sit down and my first word would be, 'Hello.' And everybody says, 'Hello.' 'I'd love to talk to you.' Then I'd go on to my spiel about staying in school and keep up their education and talked about other people that came from humble homes just like you and they made it, Ever hear of Jim Thorpe, he started just like you.

Ever hear of St. Marie, she came out of a school like yours, ever hear of Billy Mills the Olympic miler who won the mile overseas in the Olympics -- Billy Mills was a Sioux Indian. I'd go on and talk about famous Indians that have made it. "You can make it." And I told them, "I started out in an Indian School just like you and when I was 11 years old I was supposed to be assigned to the dairy, I was going to learn how -- at 11 years old they send you out to learn something, they had me on the dairy detail to go out and milk cows and had to get up at 5 o'clock in the morning. It was so early one time I over-slept in the silo. One day I slept too long and was missing for a while. They laughed over that experience that I told them. I pulled through and finally I'm in the music business now and trying to entertain you, talk to you how you too can make your life useful. And when I finished my speech, I'd get a nice, standing ovation from the kids. It was beautiful.
It sounds great, it sounds like a beautiful thing.
At all the Indian schools that was the same speech I had, some of it was written, after a while I memorized it, I did it so much, you

know. I wish I had the speech here. I did some funny things, and too, I decided to give them the facts of what I went through, there were some comical -- what did I talke about? I talked about -- oh, yes. Yes, yes. Every -- they have a Polish Day and they have a St. Patrick's Day, Irish have a St. Patrick's Day and the Italians have a church day where they carry the priest out in the square. Everybody had their holiday. I think it's about time the American Indians had a holiday, and on that holiday I venture to say it would be great to smell all the corn bread and all the beans and the fried bread on that day. We should have a day, too. They all laugh and agree with me, it was beautiful.
